title: Ibn Khaldūn’s ʿAṣabiyya — solidarity as a source of power
when: Ibn Khaldūn (1332–1406) composed the first version of the Muqaddima in 1377 and revised it over subsequent years. The term and its social meanings predate him; his distinctive analysis belongs to fourteenth-century North African scholarship.
people: Ibn Khaldūn; later interpreters debate how best to translate and apply his account of ʿaṣabiyya.
origin: The Arabic-language intellectual world of fourteenth-century North Africa, especially the scholarly and political milieu of the Maghrib.
idea: ʿAṣabiyya is often translated as group feeling, social solidarity, or esprit de corps, but no single English phrase captures its range. Ibn Khaldūn treats it as the bond that enables people to cooperate, defend one another, and pursue collective aims. Kinship can foster it, yet his account does not reduce it to shared blood: close association and alliances can widen solidarity. In the Muqaddima, this collective force helps explain how groups acquire political authority and establish dynasties. Ruling success, however, can bring settled luxury and weaken the cohesion that supported it, allowing stronger solidarities to challenge a dynasty. This is not a mechanical law that every state follows on a fixed timetable. It is a framework for asking how material conditions, social bonds, and political power interact. Scholars continue to dispute the term’s precise scope and whether modern ideas such as nationalism or social cohesion are suitable equivalents.
relevance: The concept shifts attention from leaders alone to the relationships that make coordinated action possible—and to how institutions may strengthen or erode those bonds. It remains useful for thinking about political legitimacy, collective action, and why communities hold together or fracture, while cautioning against treating solidarity as inherently benevolent: it can protect insiders and exclude outsiders.
